workedExample.problem: Clients create projects with POST /projects. After a timeout, a retry sometimes creates two projects.
steps: With POST, the service picks the ID, so a retry looks like a new create.
With PUT /projects/website-2026, the client names the project.
A repeated PUT with the same name and body has the same effect as one.
workedExample.answer: Create projects with PUT and a name the client chooses, so a retry cannot make a second project.

tradeOff.situation: Your API creates orders. Mobile clients on weak networks often time out, and then they retry.
options: Make the create call idempotent so a retry is safe
Tell clients not to retry a create call
Let clients retry, and run a nightly job that removes duplicates

reasons.text: After a timeout, the client cannot tell if it worked, so the service must make retries safe.
Fewer retries mean fewer duplicate orders, so a clear no-retry rule solves most of the problem.
A nightly clean-up job is cheap, and it removes the few duplicates that the weak networks cause.

tradeOff.explanation: A client cannot tell if a timed-out request worked, so Azure wants the service to be idempotent. The cost is extra design work, such as client-chosen names or repeatability headers.

decisionCards.situation: A client creates a project and may retry after a timeout. You choose how the project gets its name.
options: PUT with a name the client chooses
POST where the service picks the ID

reasons.text: POST is the usual way to create a resource, and most clients expect it.
Service-made IDs are unique and safe, so a retry is not a real risk here.
If the client sends the same PUT again, the same name means no second project.

decisionCards.explanation: Azure says to use PUT or PATCH to create, because the customer names the resource and the call is idempotent. But clients must then choose unique names.

screens.text: PUT and PATCH are easy to repeat. A POST that creates a resource or runs an action is harder. A retry may do the work twice. Azure wants such a POST to be retriable.

Azure says you should support OASIS Repeatable Requests. The client adds two headers to the POST: Repeatability-Request-ID and Repeatability-First-Sent. With this pair, the POST becomes safe to retry.
The service tracks the request for at least 5 minutes after the first send. An operation without this support should return 501 Not Implemented for requests with these headers.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Service: POST with both headers
  Service-->>Client: Answer lost
  Client->>Service: Same POST and same headers
  Service-->>Client: Same result

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Repeatability of requests

catch.question: Which pair of request headers makes an Azure POST safe to retry?
catch.explanation: Azure uses the OASIS Repeatable Requests headers, Repeatability-Request-ID and Repeatability-First-Sent, for POST.

card.text: In Azure, all HTTP operations are naturally idempotent, except POST to create a resource and POST for an action. To make such a POST safe to retry, Azure says you should support OASIS Repeatable Requests. The client sends Repeatability-Request-ID and Repeatability-First-Sent. The service tracks requests for at least 5 minutes after the first send. An operation without this support should return 501 Not Implemented for requests with these headers.
card.example: A client sends POST /users/Bob:grant?access=read with both repeatability headers. It retries 2 minutes later with the same headers, and the grant happens once.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Repeatability of requests

review.question: How long must an Azure service track repeatable requests?
review.answer: At least 5 minutes after the Repeatability-First-Sent time.

screens.text: Google APIs use another way to make a retry safe. A request message may have a request_id field. The guide recommends a random UUID. The field is limited to 36 ASCII characters.
Providing a request ID must guarantee idempotency. Without a request ID, the request is not idempotent. So the ID is what makes a retry safe.

If the server finds a duplicate, it should return the response of the earlier successful request. The client most likely never got that response. If it cannot be rebuilt, the server may return the current state of the resource.

catch.question: A Google API gets a duplicate request with the same request_id. What should it return?
choices: The response of the earlier successful request
catch.explanation: The client most likely did not get the first response, so the server should return it again.

card.text: Google APIs may add a request_id field to request messages. A random UUID is recommended. Providing a request ID must guarantee idempotency. If the server finds a duplicate, it should return the response of the earlier successful request. The client most likely did not get that response. Sometimes it cannot be rebuilt, because the resource changed since. Then the method may return the current state of the resource.
card.example: CreateBookRequest has a request_id field, restricted to 36 ASCII characters. The request is only idempotent when a request_id is provided.

review.question: What may a server return when the old success response cannot be rebuilt?
review.answer: The current state of the resource.

screens.text: Some work takes too long for one request. So the client starts the operation, and then calls another API to ask about its progress. This pattern is called a long-running operation, or LRO.
Azure gives a rule for when to use it. Make the operation an LRO if its 99th percentile response time is more than 1 second. So speed decides, not the method or the client.
The call that starts the work returns 202 Accepted with an operation-location header. The header holds the URL of the status monitor. The client polls that URL.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Service: POST start the work
  Service-->>Client: 202 Accepted and operation-location
  Client->>Service: GET status monitor
  Service-->>Client: Running

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Long-running operations

catch.question: When should an Azure operation be a long-running operation?
choices: When it returns more than 100 items
When the client is a mobile app
When its 99th percentile response time is over 1 second
catch.explanation: Use it when the 99th percentile response time is over 1 second. The client should also poll before it goes on.

card.text: Some operations take too long for one request. Services do not want to keep long connections open, and load balancers time out. So the client starts the operation, and then polls another API call for its progress. Use this pattern when the 99th percentile response time is over 1 second. The client should also poll before it goes on. Validate as much as you can at the start, so clients see errors early. Do not build PATCH as a long-running operation.
card.example: A client starts a reboot with POST on a VM action. It gets 202 Accepted and an operation-location URL. It polls that URL until the status is Succeeded.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Long-running operations

review.question: Why validate inputs before you start a long-running operation?
review.answer: So clients see errors early, not only after they poll.

workedExample.problem: An export call takes about 3 minutes. The load balancer drops the connection, and clients see timeouts.
steps: The call takes far more than 1 second, and the client must wait for the result, so make it long-running.
Return 202 Accepted at once, with an operation-location header.
The client polls the status monitor until the status is Succeeded or Failed.
workedExample.answer: Make the export a long-running operation: return 202 fast, and let the client poll the status.

tradeOff.situation: A report export takes about 3 minutes. Clients behind a load balancer see timeouts.
options: Raise the timeout of the load balancer to 5 minutes
Make it a long-running operation: return 202 Accepted and let the client poll
Keep one request open and ask clients to wait longer

reasons.text: A 5-minute timeout covers a 3-minute export, and the clients need no code changes.
The call takes far longer than 1 second, and such a slow call should be an LRO.
Polling sends many extra requests, so keeping one long connection open costs the server far less.

tradeOff.explanation: Azure says to use an LRO when the 99th percentile response time is over 1 second. The cost is a second API call, so the service needs a status monitor and clients must poll.

decisionCards.situation: A POST starts a VM reboot that takes much longer than 1 second. The client must know when it ends.
options: Hold the request open until the reboot ends
Return 202 Accepted with an operation-location header

reasons.text: Work that takes over 1 second should be an LRO, and the client polls it.
Holding the request open is simpler, and the client learns the end at once.
202 Accepted tells the client the reboot will succeed, so it needs no polling.

decisionCards.explanation: Azure says an operation over 1 second at the 99th percentile should be an LRO. The client then needs a second call to learn the result.

screens.text: A client starts work that takes time. The server does not want to hold the connection open. So it answers at once, before the work is finished.
The status code is 202 Accepted. It means the request was accepted for processing, but the processing is not complete.

The answer is noncommittal on purpose. The request might never be done, because it can be disallowed when processing really happens. The response should describe the current status and point to a status monitor.

catch.question: What does a 202 Accepted response say about the work?
choices: The work will surely succeed later
The request was accepted, but the processing is not complete
catch.explanation: 202 means accepted for processing, but not completed. It might still not be acted upon.

card.text: 202 Accepted means the request was accepted for processing, but the processing is not complete. The request might never be done, because it can be disallowed when processing really happens. The response is noncommittal on purpose. The client does not need to keep the connection open until the work ends. The response should describe the current status and point to a status monitor.
card.example: A batch process runs only once per day. The server answers 202 Accepted at once. The response links to a status monitor that estimates when the work will be done.

review.question: Does 202 Accepted promise that the work will succeed?
review.answer: No. It is noncommittal: the work might never be done.

screens.text: Each long-running operation has a status monitor. It is a resource with an id and a status. The status is NotStarted, Running, Succeeded, Failed or Canceled. If it is Failed, the error field gives the reason.

The client polls with GET on the monitor. The answer is 200 OK with the current state. If the operation is not complete, the response includes a retry-after header. Its value is the seconds to wait before the next poll.
Azure says to keep the monitor for at least 24 hours after the operation ends. So a client that polls late can still read the final status.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Monitor: GET status
  Monitor-->>Client: 200 OK Running and retry-after 5
  Client->>Monitor: GET status again
  Monitor-->>Client: 200 OK Succeeded

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: The status monitor resource

catch.question: A status monitor says Running. What should its GET response also include?
choices: A retry-after header with the seconds to wait
catch.explanation: While the operation is not complete, the response includes retry-after with the seconds to wait before polling again.

card.text: Each long-running operation creates a status monitor resource. It has an id and a status: NotStarted, Running, Succeeded, Failed or Canceled. If the status is Failed, the error field gives the reason. A GET on the monitor returns 200 OK with its current state. If the operation is not complete, the response has retry-after with the seconds to wait. Keep the monitor for at least 24 hours after the operation ends.
card.example: A GET on the status monitor returns 200 OK, retry-after: 5 and status Running. A later GET returns status Succeeded.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: The status monitor resource

review.question: What are the five statuses of an Azure status monitor?
review.answer: NotStarted, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Canceled.

screens.text: The client may send an Operation-Id header. It holds an ID for the status monitor. If the client sends none, the service creates one. The service returns it in the operation-id and operation-location headers.

If the Operation-Id matches an existing operation, the service fails the request with 409 Conflict. Example: a POST to /vms/vm1:reboot with operation-id: op-77 returns 202 Accepted. Another POST with op-77 gets 409 Conflict.
There is one exception: a request identical to the earlier one. The client is only retrying. So the service gives the same answer as the first time, not an error.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Service: POST reboot with op-77
  Service-->>Client: 202 Accepted
  Client->>Service: Same POST with op-77 again
  Service-->>Client: Same 202 Accepted

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Long-running operations

catch.question: A client retries the start of an operation with the same Operation-Id and an identical request. What should the service do?
choices: Treat it as a retry and return the same response
catch.explanation: An identical request with the same Operation-Id is a retry. Only a different request gets 409.

card.text: The client may pass an Operation-Id header with an ID for the status monitor. If it does not, the service creates one, usually a GUID. The service returns it in the operation-id and operation-location headers. If the Operation-Id matches an existing operation, the service fails with 409 Conflict. The exception is an identical request, because that is a retry. An identical retried POST should get the same response as the first time.
card.example: POST /vms/vm1:reboot with operation-id: op-77 returns 202 Accepted. An identical retry with op-77 gets the same response. A different request with op-77 gets 409 Conflict.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Long-running operations

review.question: When does a reused Operation-Id get 409 Conflict?
review.answer: When the request is not identical to the earlier one. An identical request is a retry.

screens.text: Teams need to share how an HTTP API works. Readers should not need the source code. OpenAPI is made for this job.

An OpenAPI Description is a standard, programming language-agnostic description of an HTTP API. People and computers can both read it. Tools use it to show documentation, generate servers and clients, and test.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[OpenAPI document] --> B[Documentation]
  A --> C[Server and client code]
  A --> D[Tests]

screens.text: Example: a description starts with openapi: 3.2.1 and an info object. The fields openapi and info are required. At least one of paths, components or webhooks must be present.

catch.question: What is an OpenAPI Description?
choices: A test suite that calls every endpoint
A standard description of an HTTP API that humans and tools can read
A list of the rate limits of an API
catch.explanation: OpenAPI defines a standard, language-agnostic description of HTTP APIs for humans and computers.

card.text: The OpenAPI Specification defines a standard, language-agnostic description of HTTP APIs. Humans and computers can understand the service without its source code or extra documentation. Tools use an OpenAPI Description to show documentation, to generate servers and clients, and to test. The document is JSON or YAML. The openapi and info fields are required. At least one of paths, components or webhooks must exist.
card.example: A description starts with openapi: 3.2.1 and an info object with the API title and version. Under paths, /pets lists the operations for pets.

review.question: Which two fields does every OpenAPI document need?
review.answer: openapi, with the specification version, and info, with metadata about the API.

workedExample.problem: The mobile team writes its API client by hand from a wiki page. The wiki is often out of date.
steps: Describe the API in one OpenAPI document.
List each path and operation, with its parameters and responses.
Let tools generate the client and the documentation from that document.
workedExample.answer: Keep one OpenAPI description as the contract, and generate the client and the docs from it.

tradeOff.situation: The mobile team writes its API client by hand from a wiki page. The wiki is often out of date.
options: Ask the backend team to update the wiki more often
Share the backend team's Postman collection with the mobile team
Keep one OpenAPI description and generate the client and docs from it

reasons.text: A wiki is easy for people to read, so better habits will keep it current.
A Postman collection holds real requests, so it shows the API better than a document.
When tools read one description, the client and docs come from the same source.

tradeOff.explanation: OpenAPI is a standard description that tools can turn into clients and documentation. The cost is that the team must keep the description correct.

decisionCards.situation: Two operations in your OpenAPI description return the same Pet object.
options: Define Pet once under components and reference it
Copy the Pet schema into each operation

reasons.text: Copies keep each operation separate, so a change for one cannot break the other.
One definition used in many places means the two responses cannot drift apart.
Objects under components apply to the operations that use them, with no reference needed.

decisionCards.explanation: The Components Object holds reusable objects, and a reference lets you use one in many places. But an object in components does nothing until something references it.

screens.text: An operation is one action on a path, such as GET on /pets. In OpenAPI, each operation can have an operationId. It is a string that identifies the operation.
The id must be unique among all operations described in the API. No two operations may share one. Tools and libraries may use it to identify the operation, so it must point to exactly one.
The id is case-sensitive. Choose a name that follows common programming naming conventions. Example: updatePetWithForm. No other operation in the API may use that id.

catch.question: What rule does OpenAPI set for operationId?
choices: It must be unique among all operations in the API
It must be in upper case
It is the same for GET and POST on one path
catch.explanation: The id must be unique among all operations described in the API, and it is case-sensitive.

card.text: Each operation can have an operationId: a string that identifies the operation. It must be unique among all operations in the API. It is case-sensitive. Tools and libraries may use it to identify the operation. So follow common programming naming conventions when you choose it.
card.example: The operation that updates a pet with form data has operationId: updatePetWithForm. No other operation in the API may use that id.

review.question: Is operationId case-sensitive?
review.answer: Yes. It must also be unique among all operations in the API.

screens.text: The Components Object holds reusable objects for the description. It has maps for schemas, responses, parameters, examples, request bodies, headers and more.
Objects in components have no effect on the API on their own. They matter only when something outside components references them. A Pet schema that nobody references does nothing.
A Reference Object points to a component. Example: $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pet'. Two operations can use it, so both share the same Pet.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Operation A] --> C[Pet schema in components]
  B[Operation B] --> C

catch.question: You define a Pet schema under components, but nothing references it. What effect does it have on the API?
catch.explanation: Objects in components have no effect unless they are referenced from outside the Components Object.

card.text: The Components Object holds reusable objects for the description. It has maps for schemas, responses, parameters, examples, request bodies, headers, security schemes and more. Objects in components have no effect on the API until something outside components references them. A Reference Object can point to one of them, so you define it once and use it in many places.
card.example: components.schemas holds a Pet schema. Two operations point to it with $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pet', so both use the same Pet.

review.question: When does an object in components affect the API?
review.answer: Only when something outside components references it.

screens.text: A service changes over time. New features ship, and old behavior may change. Many customers run code against the service all day. A change must not hurt them.

Azure sets two requirements for every service change. First, already-running customer workloads must not break. Second, customers can adopt a new service version without code changes. So avoid breaking changes.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Running workload] --> B[Service change]
  B --> C[Still works]

screens.text: A preview version ends in -preview, like 2021-06-04-preview. A preview feature must go GA, or be removed, within 1 year. The GA version must use a later date than the preview.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: API versioning

catch.question: What two requirements do the Azure guidelines set for every service change?
choices: Running customer workloads must not break, and customers can adopt a new version with no code changes
Every change needs a new URL path, and old versions stop at once
Clients must update within 90 days, and previews never end
Each change needs a major version, and minor versions are hidden
catch.explanation: Already-running workloads must not break, and customers can adopt a new version without code changes.

card.text: Services change over time. Azure sets two requirements for a change. Running customer workloads must not break. And customers can adopt a new service version without code changes. So do not introduce breaking changes. A preview version ends in -preview. A preview feature must go GA, or be removed, within 1 year. When a new preview ships, older previews may retire after at least 90 days.
card.example: A service has 2021-06-04-preview. Its GA version must use a later date. When a newer preview ships, customers on the old one get at least 90 days to upgrade.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: API versioning

review.question: How long may an Azure feature stay in preview?
review.answer: At most 1 year. Then it must go GA or be removed.

workedExample.problem: A partner calls your Azure-style API in production with a preview api-version from 14 months ago.
steps: A preview feature must go GA, or be removed, within 1 year.
Older previews may retire after a new preview ships, with at least 90 days for customers to upgrade.
A 14-month-old preview is past the 1-year limit, so it may be removed.
workedExample.answer: Move the partner to a stable, date-based api-version, because previews are short-lived.

tradeOff.situation: Your team wants a new response format for an API. Some customers parse the old format in production code.
options: Change the format for everyone now, and announce it in the release notes
Keep the old format in the current version, and ship the new format in a new api-version
Ship the new format behind a header that customers can turn off

reasons.text: Workloads that already run must not break, so the old version stays while customers move over.
Release notes give customers fair warning, and good teams read them before each update.
Customers who want the old format can turn it back with a header, so nobody breaks.

tradeOff.explanation: A new api-version lets running workloads keep working. The cost is extra work to keep two versions for a time.

decisionCards.situation: A preview feature has been in preview for 14 months. A partner still uses it in production.
options: Plan to take it to GA or remove it, and talk to the partner now
Keep it in preview with no end date, because the partner uses it

reasons.text: A preview that a partner uses in production is stable in practice, so it can stay.
The 1 year limit is for new previews, so this old one can keep going.
A preview feature has 1 year at most, then it must go GA or be removed.

decisionCards.explanation: A preview feature may live 1 year at most, so the partner needs a plan. That means a hard talk with the partner now, not later.

screens.text: A client must tell the service which version it wants. Azure does this with a query parameter. A query parameter is the part of a URL after the question mark.
The parameter is named api-version. It is required on every operation. Its value is a date in YYYY-MM-DD form. Azure puts no version number segment in the path.

Example: PUT https://service.azure.com/users/Jeff?api-version=2021-06-04. A missing api-version gets 400 with the error code MissingApiVersionParameter. An unknown value gets 400 with UnsupportedApiVersionValue.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Service: PUT /users/Jeff with no api-version
  Service-->>Client: 400 MissingApiVersionParameter

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: API versioning

catch.question: How does a client choose the version of an Azure API?
choices: With a v1 segment in the path
It cannot, because the latest version is always used
With a required api-version query parameter
catch.explanation: Every Azure operation has a required api-version query parameter. Azure puts no version in the path.

card.text: Every Azure operation has a required query parameter named api-version. The client sends it in every request, also on nextLink and operation-location URLs. Its values are dates in YYYY-MM-DD form. A missing api-version gets 400 with the error code MissingApiVersionParameter. An unknown value gets 400 with UnsupportedApiVersionValue. Azure puts no version number segment in the path.
card.example: PUT https://service.azure.com/users/Jeff?api-version=2021-06-04 uses the 2021-06-04 version. The same call with no api-version gets 400 Bad Request.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: API versioning

review.question: What happens when an Azure client leaves out api-version?
review.answer: 400 Bad Request with the error code MissingApiVersionParameter.

screens.text: A version number tells clients which API they call. Google keeps it simple. An API shows only a major version, like v1.
For REST APIs, the major version is the first part of the URI path. It never shows minor or patch numbers. So Google uses v1, not v1.0, v1.1 or v1.4.2.

Users get minor and patch changes in place, without migration. Alpha and beta channels add their level, like v1beta. A stable channel shows no level. Example: GET /v1/projects/my-project/topics HTTP/1.1.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Client] --> B[v1 stable]
  A --> C[v1beta beta]

catch.question: How do Google APIs show the version in a REST URI?
choices: As v1.4.2 at the end of the path
As v1, the first part of the path
Only as an api-version query parameter
catch.explanation: Google APIs put the major version first in the URI path. They never show minor or patch numbers.

card.text: Google APIs must have a major version number. For REST APIs, it is the first part of the URI path, like v1. They must not show minor or patch numbers: v1, not v1.4.2. Users get new features in place, with no migration. Alpha and beta channels add the level, like v1beta. Different versions must work side by side for a transition period. An old version needs a clear deprecation period before shutdown.
card.example: /v1/publishers/123/books is the stable channel. /v1beta/publishers/123/books is the beta channel. Its features are a superset of v1.

review.question: Does a Google API use v1.1 for a small change?
review.answer: No. It shows only the major version, v1, and updates it in place.

screens.text: Sometimes a breaking change to an API version is approved. Then callers must be told. Azure uses a response header for this notice.
The header is azure-deprecating. It tells people what will stop working, when, and where to learn more. It is for humans who debug or read logs. Client code is not meant to parse it.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Service response] --> B[azure-deprecating header]
  B --> C[Human reads the log]

screens.text: Example: azure-deprecating: API version 2009-27-07 will retire on 2022-12-01 (https://azure.microsoft.com/updates/video-analyzer-retirement). Send it only when the operation will stop working and the client must act.

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Deprecating behavior notification

catch.question: What is the azure-deprecating response header for?
choices: Client code parses it to switch versions
It turns off the old version at once
It tells humans what will stop working, when, and where to learn more
catch.explanation: It is for humans who read logs. It names what is deprecating, the date and a URL.

card.text: Sometimes a breaking change to an API version is approved. Then callers must be told. The response gets an azure-deprecating header. It says what is deprecating, when it will stop working, and a URL with more information. It is for humans who debug or read logs. Client code is not expected to parse it. Send it only when the operation will stop working and the client must act.
card.example: azure-deprecating: API version 2009-27-07 will retire on 2022-12-01 (https://azure.microsoft.com/updates/video-analyzer-retirement)

source.title: Azure REST API Guidelines: Deprecating behavior notification

review.question: When should a service send the azure-deprecating header?
review.answer: Only when the operation will stop working and the client must act.

screens.text: An API is a contract with its users. Users write code against it and expect it to keep working. Old clients must work with newer servers of the same major version.

Imagine a client that sends only a title when it creates a book. Now the server adds a new required field, author. This old client fails. So new required fields must not be added to existing requests.
Compatibility has three kinds. Source: old code still compiles against the new version. Wire: old code still talks correctly to a newer server. Semantic: old code still gets what developers expect.

catch.question: Which change breaks existing clients in the same major version?
choices: Adding a new required field to an existing request
Adding an optional field whose default keeps the old behavior
catch.explanation: New required fields must not be added to existing request messages or resources.

card.text: APIs are contracts with users. Users write code against an API and expect it to keep working. Old clients must work with newer servers of the same major version. You may add new methods, messages, fields or enum values. But new required fields must not be added to existing requests. A new field that clients fill needs a default that keeps the old behavior. There are three kinds of compatibility: source, wire and semantic.
card.example: A new page_size field is safe only if its default keeps the old behavior. If the default returns fewer items than before, old clients wrongly think they got all results.

review.question: May you add a new required field to an existing request?
review.answer: No. New required fields must not be added to existing requests or resources.

workedExample.problem: Your team wants to rename the field customer_name to buyer_name in the orders API.
steps: AIP-180 says renaming is the same as removing and adding.
Removing a field breaks existing clients.
So add buyer_name, keep customer_name, and specify what happens when a client sends both.
workedExample.answer: Add the new field and keep the old one. Never just rename a field in the same major version.

tradeOff.situation: Your orders API returns total as a string, and some clients parse it. A teammate wants a number instead, in the same major version.
options: Add a new number field, and keep the old string field
Change the type now, because a number is the better design
Change the type now, and accept both a string and a number on input

reasons.text: Most JSON parsers read strings and numbers alike, so the clients will hardly notice the change.
Code that depends on a field breaks when its format changes, so add a new field.
Accepting both types on input keeps old clients working, so the change is safe.

tradeOff.explanation: AIP-180 says APIs must not change the format of an existing field. The cost is that you carry two fields until the next major version.

decisionCards.situation: Nobody seems to read the field fax_number any more. You want to remove it in the same major version.
options: Remove it now, because it looks unused
Keep it until the next major version

reasons.text: Taking a field out is a backwards incompatible change, and a client may still read it.
Logs show nobody read the field for months, so removing it now breaks no one.
An optional field is not a firm promise to clients, so the team can drop it now.

decisionCards.explanation: Removing a field is a backwards incompatible change in the same major version. So an unused field stays in the API for a while.

screens.text: Your API has a field called customer_name. A teammate thinks the name is poor. They want to call it buyer_name. It looks like a small, safe change.
Renaming a field is semantically the same as remove and add. Removing a field is a backwards incompatible change. So a rename breaks clients that still send or read the old name.
Add the new name, but do not remove the old one. Here, add buyer_name and keep customer_name. If clients can send conflicting values, clearly specify what the API does.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[customer_name] --> B[Keep it]
  A --> C[Add buyer_name]

catch.question: Why is renaming a field a breaking change?
choices: It is the same as removing a field and adding a new one
New names need a new server
It is not a breaking change
catch.explanation: AIP-180 says renaming is semantically the same as remove and add, and removing breaks clients.

card.text: Existing interfaces, methods, messages, fields and enum values must not be removed in the same major version. Removing is a backwards incompatible change. Renaming is the same as remove and add. So add the new name, but do not remove the old one. If clients can now send conflicting values for the same idea, clearly specify the behavior.
card.example: To rename customer_name to buyer_name, add buyer_name and keep customer_name. Document which value wins when a client sends both.

review.question: How do you rename a field without breaking clients?
review.answer: Add the new field, keep the old one, and specify the behavior when both are sent.

screens.text: A default value is what the server sets when the client sends nothing. Example: a book has a genre field. If the client sets none, the server sets FICTION.
The default values decide the default behavior of a resource. Changing a default value is a breaking change, and it must not be done. FICTION cannot quietly become NONFICTION.
Do not change how a field with its default value is serialized either. Clients may depend on a field being present or absent. If a car had wheels with default 2, sending wheels: 2 is not compatible.

catch.question: Your API sets genre to FICTION when the client sends none. A teammate wants NONFICTION instead. What does AIP-180 say?
choices: It is fine, because defaults are not part of the contract
It is fine if you update the documentation
It is a breaking change and must not be done
It is fine for fields the server fills
catch.explanation: Changing a default value is a breaking change. The default behavior of a resource must not change.

card.text: Default values are the values the server sets when the client does not send them. They decide the default behavior of a resource. Changing a default value is a breaking change, and it must not be done. Also do not change how a field with its default value is serialized. Clients may depend on a field being present or absent.
card.example: A car has wheels with the default 2, so its JSON has no wheels field. A change that now sends wheels: 2 is not backwards compatible.

review.question: Is it safe to start sending a field that you used to leave out at its default value?
review.answer: No. Clients may depend on the field being absent.

screens.text: Code often depends on how an API behaves. Even undocumented behavior can matter. So APIs must not change visible behavior in ways that are likely to break reasonable user code.
This includes the format of a field. APIs must not change the expected format, or the way the value is built, of an existing field. It holds even for output-only fields that the service fills.
Example: ip_address held IPv4 values, and now returns IPv6. Clients that parse IPv4 break, even if the field is still a string. A format change needs a new API version.

catch.question: Your ip_address field held IPv4 values. You start to return IPv6 values in it. Is this compatible?
choices: Yes, the field type is still a string
Yes, if the field is output only
Yes, if you add a note to the docs
No, a change of the value format needs a new API version
catch.explanation: APIs must not change the format of an existing field's value within an API version, even for output-only fields.

card.text: Code often depends on API behavior, even when it is not documented. So APIs must not change visible behavior in ways that are likely to break reasonable user code. This needs judgment. Also do not change the format, or the way you build the value, of an existing field. This is true even for output-only fields that the service fills. Such a change needs a new API version.
card.example: An ip_address field always held IPv4 values. Returning IPv6 values in it breaks clients that parse IPv4, so it needs a new API version.

review.question: Is a format change in an output-only field safe?
review.answer: No. Changing the format of a field's value needs a new API version.

screens.text: The Claude API reports errors with HTTP status codes. The body is JSON with a type and a message. Example request_id in an error body: req_011CSHoEeqs5C35K2UUqR7Fy.
529 overloaded_error means the API is temporarily overloaded. It can happen when traffic is high across all users. A 429 rate_limit_error is different: your organization hit a rate limit.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  App->>API: POST request
  API-->>App: 529 overloaded_error

screens.text: Other codes: a 400 invalid_request_error is a problem with your request. A 401 authentication_error is a problem with your API key. A 500 api_error is an internal error. Every response has a request-id header for support.

catch.question: Which Claude API error means the API is temporarily overloaded?
catch.explanation: 529 overloaded_error means the API is temporarily overloaded. It can happen with high traffic across all users.

card.text: The Claude API uses HTTP status codes and returns each error as JSON with a type and a message. 400 invalid_request_error is a problem with your request. 401 authentication_error is a problem with your API key. 429 rate_limit_error means your organization hit a rate limit. 500 api_error is an unexpected internal error. 529 overloaded_error means the API is temporarily overloaded. Every response has a request-id header for support.
card.example: An error body has type error, an error object with type not_found_error and a message, and request_id req_011CSHoEeqs5C35K2UUqR7Fy.

review.question: What should you send to support about one failed Claude API call?
review.answer: Its request ID, from the request-id header or the request_id field.

workedExample.problem: Your app calls the Claude API to summarize support tickets. On busy days, some calls fail with 529, and users see an error page.
steps: 529 overloaded_error means the API is temporarily overloaded.
A temporary error is worth a retry with exponential backoff.
The official SDK retries 5xx errors twice with backoff by default, and max_retries changes this.
workedExample.answer: Treat 529 as temporary, and retry with exponential backoff, for example with the SDK's built-in retries.

tradeOff.situation: A nightly job summarizes 10000 tickets with the Claude API. Some calls fail with 529 overloaded_error.
options: Retry at once in a tight loop until the call works
Skip the failed tickets, and leave them without a summary
Retry with exponential backoff, and stop after a few tries

reasons.text: A fast retry gets the answer sooner, and one more call costs almost nothing.
A few missing summaries cost less than a nightly job that runs for hours.
A 529 is a temporary overload, so a retry after a wait is worth trying.

tradeOff.explanation: 529 is temporary, so retry with exponential backoff, as the official SDK does by default. The cost is that the job runs longer on busy days.

decisionCards.situation: A Claude API call fails with 400 invalid_request_error. Your code has a retry loop around every call.
options: Retry the same request three times
Do not retry, and fix the request

reasons.text: A retry loop is cheap insurance, and some 400 errors pass on a second try.
A 400 means the request itself is wrong, so the same request fails again.
The SDK already retries 400 errors, so the loop just matches its behavior.

decisionCards.explanation: A 400 means the request itself has a problem, so a retry sends the same problem again. Someone must look at the request and fix it now.

screens.text: Some failures are transient. Examples are a dropped connection, a rate limit, or a 5xx server error. A later try may work, so retries are useful for these.

The official SDK retries transient failures for you. By default it retries twice, with exponential backoff. It honors the retry-after header when the response has one. With backoff, each wait is longer than the last.
screens.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  App->>API: request
  API-->>App: 429 with retry-after
  App->>API: retry after the wait

screens.text: Use max_retries to change or turn off this behavior. Not every error is transient: a 400 invalid_request_error means you must fix the request. A 429 for a tier spend cap has no retry-after header.

catch.question: What does the official Claude SDK do by default after a rate limit or a 5xx error?
choices: It switches to a smaller model
It retries twice with exponential backoff, and honors retry-after
catch.explanation: The SDK retries transient failures twice by default, with exponential backoff, and honors retry-after when present.

card.text: The official SDK retries transient failures for you. These include connection errors, rate limits and 5xx server errors. It retries twice by default, with exponential backoff. It honors the retry-after header when the response has one. The max_retries setting changes or turns off this behavior. But a 429 for a tier spend cap has no retry-after header. It keeps failing until access resumes.
card.example: A script gets 429 rate_limit_error with a retry-after header, so the SDK waits and retries. A 400 invalid_request_error is not a transient failure: fix the request instead.

review.question: How many times does the official SDK retry by default?
review.answer: Twice, with exponential backoff, honoring retry-after when present.

screens.text: A normal call waits until the whole answer is ready. Then it returns one complete message. For a long answer, the user sees nothing until the end.
Set stream to true. The API then sends the response step by step as server-sent events, or SSE. The app can show text as it arrives.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[message_start] --> B[content_block_delta]
  B --> C[message_delta]
  C --> D[message_stop]

screens.text: Example: content_block_delta events carry text_delta pieces, like Hello and then !. Ping events can come at any point. An error event, like overloaded_error, can also arrive inside the stream.

catch.question: With stream set to true, how does the Claude API send the response?
choices: As one JSON body at the end
As server-sent events, step by step
catch.explanation: Setting stream to true streams the response step by step with server-sent events.

card.text: Set stream to true to get the response step by step as server-sent events. The flow is message_start, then content blocks with their deltas, then message_delta, then message_stop. Ping events can come at any point. The API may also send an error inside the stream, like an overloaded_error. New event types may be added, so your code should handle unknown types gracefully.
card.example: A stream sends content_block_delta events with text_delta pieces like Hello and then !. The app shows the text as it arrives.

review.question: Can an error arrive inside a stream?
review.answer: Yes. The API may send an error event, like overloaded_error, in the event stream.

screens.text: Some requests take a long time. Example: a very long answer with a large max_tokens. The connection can sit idle while the model works.
Some networks drop idle connections after a while. Then the request can fail with no response. For long requests, use streaming or the Message Batches API, especially over 10 minutes.

The Batches API lets you poll for results, so it needs no unbroken connection. The SDK can read a stream for you. Example: messages.stream with get_final_message and max_tokens 128000 returns the full message.
screens.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Long request] --> B[Streaming]
  A --> C[Batches API]

catch.question: You need a very long answer with a large max_tokens. What do the Claude API docs advise?
choices: Use a non-streaming call with a long timeout
Send the request twice in parallel
Use streaming or the Message Batches API
Split the answer into one call per sentence
catch.explanation: For long requests, use streaming or the Message Batches API, especially for requests over 10 minutes.

card.text: Use streaming or the Message Batches API for long requests, especially those over 10 minutes. Avoid a large max_tokens without them. Some networks drop idle connections after a while, so a request can fail with no response. The Batches API lets you poll for results, so it needs no unbroken connection. The SDKs check that a non-streaming request will not exceed a 10-minute timeout. A 504 timeout_error means the request timed out while processing.
card.example: A report job asks for up to 128000 tokens. It calls messages.stream and then get_final_message, so it still gets the complete message at the end.

review.question: Why can a long non-streaming request fail with no response?
review.answer: Some networks drop idle connections after a while.

placement.question: In resource-oriented design, what do you design first: the resources or the methods?
placement.answer: The resources, the nouns. Then their relationships and schema. The methods come last.

placement.question: What should a successful DELETE return in an Azure-style API?
placement.answer: 204 No Content, with no body. It returns 204 also when the resource does not exist.

placement.question: What is the RFC 9457 problem details format?
placement.answer: A standard JSON error body, application/problem+json, with type, title, status, detail and instance.

placement.question: Where should a non-public REST API check access?
placement.answer: At every API endpoint, with a token from a central Identity Provider.

placement.question: Which status code and header tell a client that it sends too many requests, and how long to wait?
placement.answer: 429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After header.

placement.question: Why should a list endpoint have paging from its first version?
placement.answer: The list can grow very large, and adding paging later is a breaking change.

placement.question: How does a client avoid overwriting another client's change with a PUT?
placement.answer: It sends If-Match with the ETag it read. If the resource changed, the server answers 412.

placement.question: What is an idempotency key?
placement.answer: A unique key the client sends with a request. A retry with the same key does not repeat the operation.

placement.question: Why must a service save the client token and the changes in one atomic step?
placement.answer: So it never has a token without the changes, or changes without the token.

placement.question: Why do the Azure guidelines prefer PUT over POST to create a resource?
placement.answer: PUT is idempotent and the client names the resource, so a retry cannot create a second one.

scenarios.name: The first endpoints

source.title: Slack Engineering: How we design our APIs at Slack

scenarios.problem: Your team builds the first version of a library API. The mobile team starts to use it this week.

turns.threat: The plan has endpoints like /getBook, /saveBook and /removeBookNow. Each one returns a different shape of book.
turns.constraint: No client depends on these endpoints yet, so a rewrite is still cheap.

reasons.text: The resource schema is the same in all standard methods.
Clean names alone make every endpoint return the same book.
A status code decides what shape a resource has.

moves.counterattack: Books now have clean names, but each endpoint still returns its own shape.
Creates now return 201, but the endpoints still disagree about what a book is.
The standard methods share one book schema, but you must rewrite the first endpoints.
You add 409 answers, but the book shapes still differ.

turns.modelAnswer: Model books as a resource and use the standard methods: Get, List, Create, Update and Delete. The book schema must be the same in all of them. The cost: you rewrite the first endpoints before clients depend on them.
keyPoints: Use the standard methods for most operations.
One resource schema across all methods.
Rewrite now, before clients depend on it.

turns.threat: Your create endpoint does not follow the industry standard for a create response. Developers cannot guess what it returns.
turns.constraint: Your design rule: be consistent with industry standards first.

reasons.text: An empty 200 already tells the app where the new book is.
A 201 can name the new book in its Location header.
A new custom method is the usual way to find new items.

moves.counterattack: The app reads Location and stops polling, but every create must now set Location correctly.
You add a :findNew method, and the app polls it every second instead.
You answer 409 for duplicate books, but the app still lists every second.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer a create with 201 Created and a Location header that names the new book. The app then reads that one book, with no search. The cost: every create path must set Location correctly.
keyPoints: 201 Created means a new resource exists.
The Location header names the new resource.
The client reads Location instead of searching.

turns.threat: You renamed /getBook to /books/{id}. App builds that worked yesterday get 404 today.
turns.constraint: Your rule: what worked yesterday should work tomorrow. The app only reads with the old URL.

reasons.text: A 404 with a helpful message tells the app where the book went.
Bringing back /getBook next to the new endpoint keeps the design clean.
A permanent redirect sends the app to the new URL by itself.

moves.counterattack: Book names are clean, but the old builds still get 404.
You explain the 404 in the docs, and the old builds still fail.
Old builds reach the new URL, but you must keep the old route as a redirect.
Creates return 201, but reads of /getBook still fail.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer the old URL with a permanent redirect, 301 or 308, and a Location header with the new URL. The client then loads the new URL at once. The cost: you keep the old route for the redirect.
keyPoints: A redirect has a status code that starts with 3.
The Location header names the new URL.
301 and 308 are permanent redirects.

scenarios.name: The confused client

source.title: GitHub Docs: Troubleshooting the REST API

scenarios.problem: A partner app calls your orders API. It decides what to show from your status codes.

turns.threat: The API answers 400 for broken JSON and also for a quantity of minus 3. The app shows Try again for both.
turns.constraint: The JSON is valid, but a quantity of minus 3 fails validation.

reasons.text: 422 says the request is readable but cannot be processed.
400 Bad Request is the right code for a request with a bad value.
409 fits any value that the server refuses.

moves.counterattack: You answer 409 for the quantity, but nothing conflicts, so the app is confused again.
The app can now tell a typo from a bad value, but the server must check each value.
Good orders get 201, but the two errors still look the same.

turns.modelAnswer: Keep 400 for broken syntax. Use 422 when the JSON is fine but the values cannot be processed. Then the app can show the right fix. The cost: the server must check each value and report it.
keyPoints: 400 is for a client error, like malformed syntax.
422 means correct syntax, but instructions that cannot be processed.
Different codes let the client show the right fix.

turns.threat: A script asks for many private orders of other shops. Each 403 answer tells it that the order exists.
turns.constraint: Outsiders must not even learn that a private order exists.

reasons.text: A 403 hides the order better, because it refuses access.
A 404 hides whether the order exists at all.
A 401 tells the script to stop and sign in.

moves.counterattack: The code is honest, but each 403 still tells the script that the order exists.
The script learns nothing, but partners must now check their access when they get 404.
You answer 409, and the script still learns which orders exist.
Orders get clean names, but the answers still show which ones exist.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer 404 Not Found, not 403 Forbidden, for orders the caller may not see. A 403 says that the order exists. A server may send 404 to hide that a resource exists. The cost: partners must check their access on a 404.
keyPoints: 403 means the server knows the client, but denies access.
404 can hide that a resource exists.
Partners must then check their access on a 404.

turns.threat: Two staff members create an order label with the same name at once. The second create fails, and the app shows Try again.
turns.constraint: The name was free when the user started, but another create took it first.

reasons.text: Try again works, because the next create gets a new chance.
A new method can merge the two creates by itself.
A 409 tells the user that the name is already in use.

moves.counterattack: You answer 201 for both, and now two labels share one name.
You add a :createSafely method, and it fails the same way.
The second create gets 409, and the user must pick another name.
Create returns the label now, but the second create still fails with no reason.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer the second create with 409 Conflict. The request conflicts with the current state: the name is taken. Give enough detail, so the user can see the source of the conflict. The cost: the user must pick another name.
keyPoints: 409 means a conflict with the current state.
Say what caused the conflict.
The user changes the request and sends it again.

scenarios.name: Errors nobody can read

source.title: Slack Engineering: How we design our APIs at Slack

scenarios.problem: Your shop API returns errors, but the app and the support team cannot use them.

turns.threat: Your errors have only human-readable text, with no stable code. The app picks its next step by matching those words.
turns.constraint: Your rule: errors are unambiguous, with codes next to the human-readable text.

reasons.text: Code should match a stable type URI, not human text.
A title stays the same once the API ships, so code can match it.
The status code alone tells every problem apart.

moves.counterattack: The app reads a balance field now, but it still picks the action from the title.
The errors are safer, but the app still matches on the title text.
The app checks the type URI, so titles can change, but each type URI must stay stable.
The status code is better, but many errors share it, so the app still reads titles.

turns.modelAnswer: Give each problem a type URI, and let the app decide by type. The title is only a short summary for humans. The cost: you must keep each type URI stable and documented.
keyPoints: The type URI is the main identifier of a problem.
The title is for humans, not for code.
A new type URI is a new problem identity.

turns.threat: A failed payment returns the SQL error and a full stack trace to the browser.
turns.constraint: The API is public, so anyone can make a payment fail.

reasons.text: An extension member hides data from attackers.
A stack trace shows attackers how the system is built.
A typed error is safe, even with a trace inside.

moves.counterattack: The stack trace is gone, but your team needs another way to see the cause.
You move the stack trace into an extension, so attackers still read it.
The error has a type now, but the stack trace is still in the body.

turns.modelAnswer: Remove implementation details, like stack dumps, from the response. The detail text should help the client fix the problem. The cost: developers need another way to see the cause.
keyPoints: Error details can help attackers.
Do not show a stack dump through the HTTP interface.
The detail text helps the client fix the problem.

turns.threat: Your SDK turns every error into Request failed. It throws away the HTTP headers and the raw body.
turns.constraint: The error type is in the body, and the wait time is in a header.

reasons.text: A clear status line makes the headers and the body extra.
Error bodies matter to the server team, but SDK users can skip them.
The status code alone carries neither the type nor the wait time.

moves.counterattack: Developers see 429 Too Many Requests, but the wait time is still lost.
The body has a type URI, but the SDK still throws the body away.
Developers get the full error, but the SDK error object grows bigger.
The detail is safe now, but nobody sees it.

turns.modelAnswer: A response has a status line, headers and an optional body. Each part can carry data the developer needs. So pass all three on in the SDK error. The cost: the error object grows bigger.
keyPoints: A response has a status line, headers and a body.
Error details can sit in the headers and the body.
Do not let the SDK throw them away.

scenarios.name: The leaked key

source.title: RubyGems Blog: API key logging leak

scenarios.problem: API keys leaked through your access logs. Your team checks how keys and tokens travel.

turns.threat: Your access logs go to an outside service. They hold full URLs with API keys in the query string.
turns.constraint: The logs keep every full URL, and these API clients can send headers.

reasons.text: Logs store full URLs, so a key in a URL gets stored too.
HTTPS encrypts the whole URL, so the key stays out of the server logs.
Failed requests are the ones that end up in the logs.

moves.counterattack: Keys are safe on the network now, but the URLs in the logs still hold them.
Keys move to a header and leave the logs, but every client must change its calls.
Error bodies are cleaner, but the keys still sit in the URLs.

turns.modelAnswer: Move API keys out of the URL and into a header. Web server logs capture URLs, so keys there leak. The cost: every client must change how it sends the key.
keyPoints: Never put keys or tokens in the URL.
Logs capture URLs.
Send keys in a header.

turns.threat: With two-factor authentication on, a valid API key is not enough to push a gem. The push tool asks for a new key again and again.
turns.constraint: The key is valid; this action also needs the second factor.

reasons.text: A 401 and a 403 mean the same thing to a client tool.
A 401 asks for new credentials, so the tool asks for a key again.
A 409 tells the tool to stop and wait.

moves.counterattack: Keys are out of the URL, but the app still loops on 401.
The app gets 409 now, and it retries the same request.
The traffic is encrypted, but the sign-in loop goes on.
The sign-in loop stops, but the app now needs a clear no-access screen.

turns.modelAnswer: The token is valid, so answer 403 Forbidden, not 401. A 401 tells the client to try new credentials. The client should not repeat a 403 with the same credentials. The cost: the app needs a no-access screen.
keyPoints: 401 means missing or invalid credentials.
403 means valid credentials, but no access.
Clients should not repeat a 403 with the same credentials.

turns.threat: A teammate says API keys in the query string are fine, because HTTPS encrypts the URL on the network.
turns.constraint: Your Nginx and CDN access logs store the full request URL, query string included.

reasons.text: HTTPS keeps the URL encrypted in the logs as well.
Access logs store the path of each request, but they drop the query string.
The request target is part of the request line that gets logged.

moves.counterattack: The network is safe, but the logs still store the full request line.
Error bodies are safe, but the keys still sit in the logs.
The team sees why the logs hold keys, but every client must move its key out of the URL.
The status codes are right, but the logs still hold the keys.

turns.modelAnswer: The first line of an HTTP/1.x request is the request line: method, request target and protocol. The request target is usually a URL. So a log of request lines also holds any key in that URL. The cost: clients must move their keys.
keyPoints: The request line has a method, a target and a protocol.
The request target is usually a URL.
A log of request lines stores keys in URLs.

scenarios.name: The greedy partner

source.title: Stripe Blog: Scaling your API with rate limiters

scenarios.problem: One partner's integration sends more requests than all the other partners together.

turns.threat: During an incident, your servers cannot serve all regular traffic. Low-priority calls crowd out critical calls, like new payments.
turns.constraint: The overload is on your side, and no single user sends too fast.

reasons.text: The cause is your own overload, not one client's speed.
A 429 is the right answer to an overload of any kind.
Each request should wait the same, so no call gets dropped.

moves.counterattack: Fast keys get 429, but the overload is yours, so careful partners get blamed too.
You send a wait time, but every kind of call still fights for the same servers.
New payments get through, but some low-priority calls fail with 503 until the servers recover.

turns.modelAnswer: Answer the low-priority calls with 503 Service Unavailable, so payments get through. A 503 means the server is not ready, for example from too much traffic. Use it for temporary conditions. The cost: some calls fail for a while.
keyPoints: 503 says the server is not ready for now.
429 is for a client that sends too many requests.
Drop low-priority calls first, so payments get through.

turns.threat: One user is responsible for a spike in traffic. Calls from every other user slow down.
turns.constraint: One API key causes the spike, and every other user pays for it.

reasons.text: A wait header makes a fast client slow down by itself.
A limit per key stops one user from slowing everyone.
Moving the key to a header lowers the request rate.

moves.counterattack: You send Retry-After, but with 200 OK answers the partner has no reason to wait.
The key moves to a header, and it still sends 300 requests per second.
The key gets 429 above its limit, but you must agree on a limit with each partner.
You answer 409, but nothing conflicts, and the partner retries at once.

turns.modelAnswer: Limit requests per API key, and answer 429 Too Many Requests when a key goes too fast. Revoke a key that keeps breaking the usage agreement. The cost: each partner needs a clear, agreed limit.
keyPoints: Require an API key on every request.
Return 429 when a key sends too fast.
Revoke a key that breaks the agreement.

turns.threat: A user's misbehaving script hits the limit. It retries at once, again and again, all night.
turns.constraint: The script can slow down without changing its result, if it knows how long to wait.

reasons.text: A smoother bucket stops a script that retries at once.
A wait field in the error body reaches each client.
Retry-After tells the client how long to wait.

moves.counterattack: The script now waits the time you send, but you must choose a fair wait.
Capacity refills smoothly, but the script still hits you between refills.
The key moves to a header, and the script still retries at once.

turns.modelAnswer: Send a Retry-After header, so the client knows how long to wait. The value is seconds or an HTTP date. The cost: you must choose a wait that is fair and correct.
keyPoints: Retry-After says how long to wait.
It is a number of seconds or an HTTP date.
The client waits before its next request.

scenarios.name: The endless list

source.title: Slack Engineering: Evolving API Pagination at Slack

scenarios.problem: An endpoint was designed for a few hundred records. Now it returns hundreds of thousands.

turns.threat: GET /orders returns every order in one response. Mobile apps wait a long time for it.
turns.constraint: Clients must still be able to reach every order, page by page.

reasons.text: A nextLink lets the client fetch pages until none is left.
A smaller page size shows clients where the rest of the list is.
Fewer calls per minute make each response smaller.

moves.counterattack: Clients can ask for fewer orders, but nobody knows how to get the rest.
Pages come fast with a nextLink, but old clients that expect every order break.
You limit the calls, but each call is still huge and slow.
You add an :exportAll method, but it still returns everything.

turns.modelAnswer: Return the list in pages, with a nextLink to the next page and no nextLink on the last one. The cost: adding paging later is a breaking change, so old clients must change.
keyPoints: Lists that can grow need paging.
nextLink points to the next page.
Adding paging later breaks old clients.

turns.threat: A task app calls users.list again and again to retrieve all users. A teammate fears that the repeated calls change data.
turns.constraint: The list call is a GET, and it only reads users.

reasons.text: Each repeated call needs an idempotency key to be safe.
A safe method only reads, so repeated calls change nothing.
Repeated list calls can move the cursor on the server and skip users.

moves.counterattack: Keys work, but this read-only call never needed one.
The app keeps calling, but your servers still log and count every call.
The token stays opaque, but the teammate still fears the calls.
Calls spread out, but nobody knows yet if they change data.

turns.modelAnswer: GET is a safe method: it does not change the state of the server. It is read-only. So repeated list calls change no data. The cost: the server can still log or count the calls.
keyPoints: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe.
Safe means read-only.
The server can still log or count calls.

turns.threat: A partner decodes your Base64 page token and edits what is inside. After you change the token, their app shows the wrong orders.
turns.constraint: You want to change how paging works inside the token next month.

reasons.text: Base64 encoding is enough to keep a page token opaque to clients.
A nextLink hides the token from the partner.
Clients who can read a token come to depend on what is inside.

moves.counterattack: Tokens become truly opaque, but this partner must rewrite its paging code.
You send a nextLink, but it carries the same readable token, so the partner keeps editing it.
Keys leave the URL, but the token is still easy to edit.

turns.modelAnswer: Page tokens must be opaque. If users can take them apart, they will, and then you cannot change your paging. Base-64 encoding alone is not enough. The cost: partners who decoded tokens must change their code.
keyPoints: Page tokens must be opaque.
Base-64 encoding alone is not enough.
Readable tokens freeze your paging design.

scenarios.name: Two editors
scenarios.problem: Support agents change the same records through your API. It follows the Azure guidelines, where ETags offer optimistic concurrency.

turns.threat: Two agents change one record at the same time. The second save erases the first agent's change.
turns.constraint: Each agent's app keeps the ETag of the record that it read.

reasons.text: If-Match lets the server refuse a save based on old data.
If-None-Match protects saves as well as reads.
A 409 alone tells the server which save used old data.

moves.counterattack: You return 409 sometimes, but the server cannot tell which save used old data.
If-None-Match with an ETag guards reads, so saves still overwrite each other.
The customer list pages well, but saves still overwrite each other.
Saves based on old data now fail with 412, but agents must reload and redo their change.

turns.modelAnswer: Send If-Match with the ETag the agent read. If the customer changed since, the server must not apply the save, and it answers 412. The cost: the agent must reload and redo the change.
keyPoints: If-Match carries the ETag the client read.
A changed resource gets 412, not a silent overwrite.
This prevents the lost update problem.

turns.threat: An agent's save times out, so the app is not sure if it worked. The app drops the change and shows an error.
turns.constraint: Your guidelines say every operation is idempotent, so clients can retry.

reasons.text: A save that timed out has to be checked by hand.
An idempotent request can be sent again with the same effect.
A retry is safe after the agent reloads the page, not before.

moves.counterattack: You switch the save to POST, which is not guaranteed to be idempotent.
The app retries the save, but each response may differ.
Reads are cheaper, but the save is still dropped.
Pages get smaller, but the save is still dropped.

turns.modelAnswer: A request is idempotent if several identical requests have the same intended effect as one. A client can safely retry it when it is not sure the request arrived. So the app retries the save. The cost: the response can still differ between calls.
keyPoints: Identical requests have the same effect as one.
A client can retry an idempotent request.
The response can still differ.

turns.threat: An update worked, but its reply was lost. The identical retry is now seen as a conflict.
turns.constraint: The ETag is the record's version number.

reasons.text: A version number is the most precise ETag, so retries can trust it.
If-None-Match lets an update retry pass.
A hash of the whole resource stays the same for an identical retry.

moves.counterattack: The retry gets a clearer 409, but it is still rejected.
A hash of the resource helps retries, but you must hash the whole resource on each change.
If-None-Match does not help an update retry, so it still fails.

turns.modelAnswer: Azure prefers a hash of the whole resource as the ETag, not a version number. A version number can make a retried update look like a conflict. The cost: you compute a hash on each change.
keyPoints: Return an ETag with each read and update.
Prefer a hash of the whole resource.
Version numbers can break retries.

scenarios.name: The double charge

source.title: Stripe Blog: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

scenarios.problem: Your payment service accepts idempotency keys. Networks fail, so clients are often unsure whether a call worked.

turns.threat: A client creates a DNS record with PUT, and the connection breaks. A teammate wants an idempotency key on this call too.
turns.constraint: The PUT carries all the information needed to create the record.

reasons.text: Identical PUT requests have the same effect as one.
An idempotency key is needed for each kind of retry.
A POST is safer to retry than a PUT.

moves.counterattack: Keys work, but you now store responses for a call that was already safe.
You switch to POST, and now a retry may create the record twice.
Retries of the PUT are safe as they are, but each response may still differ.
The client waits longer before it retries, but nobody knows if a retry is safe.

turns.modelAnswer: PUT is idempotent: identical requests have the same intended effect as one. So the client can retry it safely after a failure. POST is not guaranteed to be idempotent. The cost: the response can still differ between calls.
keyPoints: PUT and DELETE are idempotent.
A client can retry an idempotent request safely.
POST is not guaranteed to be idempotent.

turns.threat: A charge call fails with a network error. The shop app makes a new key for the retry, and the customer pays twice.
turns.constraint: The retry is for the same charge, after a network error.

reasons.text: A new key for the retry is safer, because it starts clean.
Only the same key lets the service return the first result.
If-Match stops a second payment.

moves.counterattack: Mismatched retries now fail, but a new key still looks like a new payment.
A retry with the same key gets the saved first response, but a saved 500 also comes back.
A payment is not an update, so If-Match does not stop the second charge.

turns.modelAnswer: Keep the same key for every retry of one payment. The service saves the first response and returns it to retries. The cost: as in Stripe API v1, a saved error, even a 500, comes back to every retry.
keyPoints: Retry with the same key, never a new one.
The first result is saved and returned.
In Stripe API v1, saved errors come back too.

turns.threat: A bug in one shop app reuses one key for every order of the day. Later orders get the first order's receipt.
turns.constraint: Different orders arrive with the same key on the same day.

reasons.text: Keys that expire after a day stop the mix-up.
The saved response is a safe answer to any reuse of a key.
A key belongs to one request, so other parameters are an error.

moves.counterattack: Keys expire after a day, but orders on the same day still share one receipt.
Each order says 201, but later orders still get the first receipt.
The saved response is exactly what returns the first receipt to later orders.
A reused key with a new order now gets an error, but that shop app must fix its key bug.

turns.modelAnswer: Compare the parameters with the first request that used this key. Different parameters with the same key get an error, not a saved response. The cost: the app with the bug must create one key per order.
keyPoints: Compare the parameters with the first request of the key.
Same key and different parameters: return an error.
A key recognizes retries of the same request.

scenarios.name: The ghost servers

source.title: Amazon Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs

scenarios.problem: Your cloud service creates servers for customers. Their scripts retry every failed call.

turns.threat: A launch call gets no response, perhaps because of a network timeout. A teammate wants scripts to send it again at once.
turns.constraint: The launch call is a plain POST, and it carries no client token yet.

reasons.text: A repeated POST may start a second server.
The HTTP client retries each request safely by itself.
A timeout means that the server did not start.

moves.counterattack: You call the launch idempotent, but a repeated POST can still start a second server.
You plan to keep tokens longer, but these calls carry none.
The scripts stop blind repeats, but each retry now needs a check first.

turns.modelAnswer: POST is not idempotent. Identical POST requests may have extra effects, like creating the same thing twice. So a blind repeat of the launch is not safe. The cost: each retry needs a check first.
keyPoints: POST is not idempotent.
A repeated POST may create a second resource.
Do not repeat it blindly.

turns.threat: Retries get ResourceAlreadyExists. Customer scripts think someone else made the server, and they stop.
turns.constraint: Customer scripts treat ResourceAlreadyExists as another person's server.

reasons.text: Keeping tokens longer changes what a retry hears.
Every retry with the same token should get the first answer.
A typed error tells the script that it was its own server.

moves.counterattack: You switch to 409, and the scripts still think someone else made it.
Retries get the same answer as the first call, but you must keep the data for that answer.
You keep tokens longer, but retries still get ResourceAlreadyExists.
The error now has a type, but it is still the wrong answer to a retry.

turns.modelAnswer: Return a semantically equivalent response to every retry with the same token. The script gets the same server ID, as if no retry happened. The cost: the service must keep enough data to rebuild that answer.

ResourceAlreadyExists confuses the caller.
Then SDKs can retry for you.

turns.threat: Your service saves the client token, then crashes before it creates the server. Retries now say success, but no server exists.
turns.constraint: The service can crash between any two steps of a create.

reasons.text: Saving the response with the token keeps the token and the server together after a crash.
Expired tokens clean up a broken create quickly.
A token and a server saved in one step cannot be split by a crash.

moves.counterattack: You save the response too, but a crash can still split the token from the server.
The broken token expires after a day, so customers wait a day for a server.
Token and server are saved together now, but every create runs in one transaction.

turns.modelAnswer: Save the token and all changes in one ACID operation, all or nothing. Then a crash leaves neither a token without a server nor a server without a token. The cost: each create runs inside one transaction.
keyPoints: The token and the changes are saved together.
All or nothing, as one ACID operation.
No token without the resource.

scenarios.name: The twin grants

source.title: Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

scenarios.problem: Workers call your services in parallel. Each worker retries a call that fails or times out.

turns.threat: A grant call with a side effect times out. The worker retries it, and access is granted twice.
turns.constraint: The service recognizes a repeated POST by its Repeatability-Request-ID header.

reasons.text: Repeatability-Request-ID lets the service run a repeated POST once.
Comparing parameters stops an exact retry.
If-Match also stops a repeated action that has no ETag.

You compare parameters, but an exact retry still runs twice.
The grant returns 201, but it still runs twice.
If-Match blocks a second change of the same version, but actions with no ETag still repeat.

turns.modelAnswer: Support the repeatability headers on the POST action. A retry with the same Repeatability-Request-ID is recognized and runs once. The cost: the service must track requests for at least 5 minutes.

Repeatability-Request-ID marks the retry.
Track requests for at least 5 minutes.

turns.threat: Several workers send the same create call. Each call creates one more book.
